It depends on what I'm doing. If I'm managing credentials for personal accounts, I use KeePassX or LastPass. If I'm stashing my porn, I use GnuPG. I don't know any reason not to use openssl for these purposes, and if you're already using it for other purposes then maybe you'll prefer it.

When it comes to encryption, I think the two most important things are the algorithm and the keys. Both programs allow you to select your algorithm, and in either case protecting the keys is still up to the user.

It depends on what you're encrypting and why.

When I do full system-disk encryption, I use Cryptab. It's built into Systemd, and that garbage is on almost all Linux systems now. It's secure, easy to use, and works great with LVM. You can copy/restore/delete your header files in the event you need to "permanently lock" your system.

For full (removable) disk encryption, I use Veracrypt with AES. It's a multi-government standard, and about as good as encryption gets. Veracrypt is active, o.en-sourced, and stable. It's easy to use, and it's never given me any problems.

When I do E-mails, or send files, I use PGP... Which is just AES using public/private keys. Same level of security, same compression rate, and same sender assurance. But this allows me to sign messages to authenticate it's coming from me.

As for texts, I use Signal, which is just another implementation of AES for your SMS/MMS. I can guarantee that a message is coming from, or going to, the determined destination.
